headline: Tex-Mex is a birthright here, served on flour tortillas and argued over at drive-ins
summary: San Antonio eats Mexican-American first, from a Tejano and Chicano lineage older than the skyline: the plaza Chili Queens, the Market Square panaderías, the West Side drive-ins. Breakfast tacos come on flour tortillas and barbacoa comes on Sunday. The places people defend are family-run and decades old. For the 2026 Finals runners-up, food is the shortest road from the court to the neighborhood table.

insights.title: The puffy taco could only be San Antonio
insights.detail: Fried-masa puffy tacos belong to the West Side drive-in tradition. Locals argue over Ray's Drive Inn and Henry's Puffy Tacos. Breakfast tacos on flour tortillas (bean and cheese, potato and egg, migas) are the daily ritual on every block.
insights.implication: A puffy-taco silhouette or a breakfast-taco foil-wrap graphic reads as insider in a way a generic taco icon never would. Keep it a small graphic or hangtag detail, not a costume.

insights.title: Mexican-American families built the table
insights.detail: Mi Tierra at Market Square, the panadería counters and the Christmas tamalada tradition come from Tejano and Mexican-American families who built the city's food economy. Spurs fandom in South Texas and across the border in Mexico overlaps heavily with this table.
insights.implication: Partner with San Antonio Latino chefs, bakers and illustrators, and credit them. Don't lift their imagery. The community authors the cues, so pay it.

insights.title: H-E-B and Whataburger are civic brands you can wear
insights.detail: H-E-B is headquartered in San Antonio, and people wear its Texas-pride merchandise with sincerity. Whataburger, also headquartered here, has a fan-merch culture of its own, with its orange-and-white A-frame and stripes.
insights.implication: Both are third-party trademarks, so any reference needs a licensed collaboration. A co-branded capsule would carry local weight, but only through formal licensing.

insights.title: Fiesta feeds the city as the playoffs start
insights.detail: Fiesta runs through April with its medals, papel picado and cascarones. A Night in Old San Antonio and the Oyster Bake bring the food. The Spurs' Fiesta-stripe City Edition already borrows the palette, and the playoffs run April to June.
insights.implication: Plan a Fiesta-week product and content drop for April. Let the City Edition story live in food and street color, not only on the court.

insights.title: Ice houses, not sports bars, are where neighborhoods gather
insights.detail: Open-air Texas ice houses like the Friendly Spot in Southtown play host to the beer, tacos and TV watch party. Food trucks park beside the picnic tables. Game nights spill into patios, taquerias and backyards.
insights.implication: Run watch parties at ice houses and taquerias with local food trucks. Design for patio weather: lightweight, sun-ready, easy to layer.

insights.title: The Pearl and Southtown carry the chef-driven layer
insights.detail: New chef-led spots cluster at the Pearl, anchored by the Culinary Institute of America campus and a Saturday farmers market, and in Southtown's restaurant and bar scene. Steve McHugh and Johnny Hernandez are the recognized voices.
insights.implication: Use the Pearl for premium and press-facing moments. Pair it with West Side and East Side family spots, so the story isn't all polish. Don't let the Pearl stand in for the whole city.

places.name: Mi Tierra Café y Panadería
places.why: A long-running family institution at El Mercado, known for all-hours service, a pan dulce case and a ceiling of papel picado and lights.

places.name: Ray's Drive Inn
places.why: A West Side drive-in tied to the puffy taco's origin story and a pillar of the neighborhood's food identity.

places.name: Henry's Puffy Tacos
places.why: The other family name in the puffy taco conversation, and a long-standing rival claim to the dish.

places.name: Los Barrios
places.why: A decades-old family Tex-Mex institution led by chef Diana Barrios Treviño, known for cabrito and family-recipe dishes.

places.name: Pearl (former Pearl Brewery) and Pearl Farmers Market
places.why: A converted brewery campus with the Culinary Institute of America, chef-driven restaurants and a Saturday market.

places.name: The Friendly Spot Ice House
places.why: A covered-patio ice house with food trucks, picnic tables and screens. It's the archetype of the local watch party.

places.name: Market Square (El Mercado)
places.why: The historic Mexican marketplace, where the city's Mexican-American food and craft culture is on display year-round.

places.name: Frost Bank Center
places.why: Home court. The pregame meal usually happens in the lots, taquerias and ice houses around it, not inside.

people.name: Johnny Hernandez
people.role: chef and restaurateur (La Gloria, True Flavors)
people.why: A prominent San Antonio chef whose restaurants celebrate Mexican street food. He's active in big local food events.

people.name: Steve McHugh
people.why: A nationally recognized chef at the Pearl who anchors the Texas-ingredient, chef-driven wave.

people.name: Diana Barrios Treviño
people.why: Carries a multi-generation Tex-Mex family restaurant tradition and is a respected voice on the city's Mexican food heritage.

people.name: H-E-B
people.why: A beloved civic brand with its own wearable pride culture. Any use needs a license.

people.name: Whataburger
people.why: A cult Texas brand with orange-and-white stripes and an enthusiastic merch following. Licensing is required.

moments.name: Fiesta San Antonio
moments.why: A ten-day citywide celebration of food, color and parades, overlapping the start of the NBA playoffs.

moments.name: A Night in Old San Antonio (NIOSA)
moments.why: The multi-night Fiesta food festival at La Villita, run by the Conservation Society, with dozens of food booths.

moments.name: Fiesta Oyster Bake
moments.why: A long-running Fiesta event with food, music and a student-and-community crowd.

moments.name: Opening night vs OKC
moments.why: A West finals rematch and the season's first meal-and-watch ritual.

moments.name: Dia de Muertos season
moments.why: Pan de muerto and ofrendas fill panaderías and Market Square. This is a sensitive cultural moment, so work only with partners.

moments.name: Tamalada and Christmas tamale season
moments.why: Families gather to make tamales, and the Dec 25 Spurs game at the Knicks lands in the middle of it.

moments.name: Spurs home-game ritual
moments.timing: Every home game, Oct to Apr
moments.why: Tacos, tailgating and ice-house stops come before tip-off.

vocabulary.meaning: A fried fresh-masa shell that puffs and crisps. The city's signature taco.
Egg, potato, bean, chorizo or migas in a flour tortilla. The daily staple.
Mexican sweet bread (conchas, marranitos, orejas) bought at the panadería.
Slow-cooked meat, traditionally a weekend family meal with tortillas.
Open-air Texas neighborhood bar with picnic tables and a food truck.
Confetti-filled eggshells cracked over heads during Fiesta.
The team's rally cry, shouted in every restaurant on game night.
The regional Mexican-American cuisine of South Texas, which San Antonio treats as its own.

designCues.cue: Fiesta stripe palette: hot pink, marigold and turquoise stripes against Spurs black
designCues.source: Fiesta medals, papel picado and the City Edition's Fiesta-colored stripes
designCues.use: Use as a stripe or trim system. Keep black dominant, so it reads Spurs first and Fiesta second.

designCues.source: Corn masa, fried puffy-taco shells, marigolds on Day of the Dead altars
designCues.use: Accent in heat-transfer or embroidery on black or silver bases.

designCues.source: The pan dulce case at any panadería
designCues.use: A soft secondary colorway for lifestyle and women's pieces. Name it with a bakery reference.

designCues.source: Market Square and Fiesta decorations; a Mexican folk craft
designCues.use: Tonal laser-cut or perforated detailing on sleeves or linings. Commission local papel picado artists.
Tiny sock, tag or insole graphic, drawn by a San Antonio illustrator.
Crinkle foil finish on a packaging or hang-tag element. Tan kraft bag print for a shirt box.

designCues.cue: Ice-house bottle-cap and neon sign lettering
designCues.use: Hand-lettered script and neon-tube outlines for graphic tees.
Keep silver as the anchor, so food cues stay accents.

productHooks: Fiesta-week capsule timed to April: stripe-trim tees and warm-ups in the City Edition palette, with a papel picado tonal print developed with a San Antonio artist.
Taquería-to-tip-off graphic tee line (puffy taco, breakfast taco, concha), illustrated by local Latino artists with credit on the tag.
Licensed H-E-B or Whataburger collaboration capsule, pursued only through the brands' own licensing teams.
Packaging that nods to the taquería: foil-wrap shoe-box liner and kraft-bag tags, limited to local launch events.
Ice-house watch-party kit (patio-weight hoodie, cap, koozie) for Spurs playoff runs.
watchouts: Don't caricature Mexican-American culture. Avoid sombreros, mustaches and mariachi tropes, and commission and credit San Antonio Latino creators.
H-E-B, Whataburger, Mi Tierra and any restaurant name or logo are third-party marks. Get licensing or permission.
Day of the Dead and Lotería imagery are cultural, and Lotería is also commercially owned. Use them only with community partners and rights holders.
Don't call the puffy taco's origin settled. Several families dispute it.
